questions.stem: A 36-year-old man presented unwell with a 2-week history of fever and new-onset intense myalgia. He also initially had abdominal pain, diarrhea, and vomiting. He was usually well and did not take any regular medications. He was a nonsmoker and did not take any recreational drugs. He had arrived in the United States 3 weeks earlier from rural Mexico. For his farewell party his friends in Mexico prepared for him smoked boar meat. On examination, his temperature was 38.5°C, his heart rate was 110 beats/minute, his respiratory rate was 26 breaths/minute, and his oxygen saturations were 93% on room air. He had periorbital edema and conjunctivitis, respiratory distress with bibasal crackles, and peripheral edema. Investigations: CPK 512 U/L EKG: flat T waves in I, AVL, V5, and V6 Cardiac MR: gadolinium enhancement in the lateral and inferolateral epicardial areas
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Trichinellosis This patient most likely has trichinellosis with myocarditis as a disease manifestation. He likely acquired Trichinella spiralis from consumption of undercooked boar meat. Clinically relevant clues to the diagnosis include the ingestion of undercooked boar, the GI syndrome followed by intense myalgia and fever, as well as periorbital edema and conjunctivitis. Although enteroviral and influenza myocarditis can present with a viral prodrome and malaise, the myalgias would be milder, and there would not be associated facial edema. Although the ECG findings and elevated enzymes would fit a diagnosis of lateral wall MI, the additional symptoms and findings would not be explained by this diagnosis. While Brucella is present in wild boar meat, most infections are due to skinning and meat handling, and the symptoms of myocarditis do not fit the clinical presentations of brucellosis.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q16

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man presented with a 24-hour history of an excruciating headache, photophobia, and neck stiffness. The headache had been gradual in onset, progressing in severity. Seven days earlier he had returned from a 2-month holiday in Vietnam where he had been staying with family. He had a history of hypertension and osteoarthritis of his knees and took regular amlodipine. Investigations: Peripheral white blood cell count 7.3 ×109/L Peripheral eosinophil count 1.5 ×109/L CSF white cell count 346 ×106/L; 30% eosinophils CSF red cell count 22 ×106/L CSF protein 560 mg/L CSF/plasma glucose 3.5/4.8 mmol/L CSF microscopy: no organisms seen CT head with contrast – mild leptomeningeal enhancement
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely source of the infecting organism?
questions.explanation: Consumption of undercooked snails The infective organism is most likely to be Angiostrongylus cantonensis, the rat lungworm. This is due to the geographical exposure (SE Asia), the incubation period (average 10 days), the clinical features (excruciating progressive headache), and the eosinophilic meningitis without raised red cells. The commonest source of A. cantonensis is consumption of raw or undercooked snails.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q12

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman presented with high fevers, severe muscle pain, tenderness, and swelling. There was no significant past medical history. There were no other symptoms reported, no recent unusual activities, although she did recall eating some undercooked pork 3 weeks previously. On examination her temperature was 38.6 oC. She was tender and had limited movement due to pain in the muscles of her shoulder girdle, upper arms, and forearms. There were numerous subungual splinter hemorrhages seen, and she had bilateral conjunctival hemorrhages. Mild hepatomegaly was palpable. Investigations: Total white cell count 13.2 ×109/L Eosinophil count 4.1 ×109/L
questions.lead_in: What parasite is most likely to be responsible?
questions.explanation: Trichinella spiralis The most likely diagnosis is infection with Trichinella spiralis, a tissue nematode. It is transmitted through ingestion of raw or undercooked contaminated meat (encysted larvae). Muscle stage develops when intestinal adult-derived larvae disseminate hematogenously (or via lymphatics) and invade striated muscle.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q19

questions.stem: A 46-year-old Thai woman presented with a sudden onset headache and right-sided weakness. Her temperature was 36.5°C, blood pressure 124/74 mmHg, and heart rate 88 beats/ minute. Her Glasgow Coma Score was 14/15. She was drowsy but rousable. She had a right-sided flaccid hemiparesis. An urgent CT scan of her head was arranged. Investigations: Eosinophils 5.9 ×109/L CT scan of head: On further questioning her partner revealed that she had also had a prolonged history of recurrent superficial swellings on her arms and torso. These would last for 1–2 weeks, resolve then recur weeks to months later. She had been born and brought up in a small village in northern Thailand, but had emigrated 6 years previously. She had spent 3 months of each year since then in Thailand.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely source of her infection?
questions.explanation: Uncooked freshwater fish This is a clinical case of gnathostomiasis, evidenced by the recurrent cutaneous swellings, the epidemiologic risk factors associated with Thailand, and the investigative findings. Gnathostoma spinigerum is acquired by eating undercooked infected poultry, snake, or freshwater fish, or by drinking water contaminated with infected Cyclops crustaceans. (Image from Assessments. In Cohen J, Powderly W , Opal S, eds. Infectious Diseases. 4th ed. Elsevier; 2017.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q42

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman presented with migratory swellings over her right arm and back. They typically lasted for 1–3 days and were hot, red, painful, and itchy. She had returned 4 weeks earlier from a 12-month job in Cameroon. A presumptive diagnosis of loiasis was made, pending investigations.
questions.lead_in: What was the most likely vector for her infection?
questions.explanation: Chrysops deerfly This is the vector responsible for the transmission of Loa loa, with the female of the species biting during the day, especially in the wet season.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q50

questions.model_answer:
a) Wuchereria bancrofti (lymphatic filariasis).
b) Adult worms residing in lymphatic vessels cause lymphatic dilatation, valvular incompetence and dysfunction; the resulting impaired lymph flow (worsened by worm death, host inflammatory/granulomatous response and secondary bacterial infection) produces lymphedema of the leg and scrotum/hydrocele.
c) (1) Circulating filarial antigen assay (ICT card/Og4C3 ELISA, W. bancrofti). (2) Nocturnal (10 pm-2 am) thick blood smear for microfilariae. (3) Scrotal/lymphatic ultrasound ("filarial dance sign") or PCR/serology.
d) Streptococcus pyogenes (group A Streptococcus), causing acute dermatolymphangioadenitis (ADLA).
e) (1) Rigorous limb hygiene and foot/skin care with treatment of interdigital tinea/entry lesions. (2) Decongestive measures - compression, elevation, exercise to promote lymph flow. (3) Prophylactic antibiotics for recurrent attacks (oral penicillin or benzathine penicillin IM).

cohort_answer.text:
Most likely organism: Wuchereria bancrofti
Mechanism for edema: Redbook: Adult worms cause lymphatic dilatation and dysfunction, which result in abnormal lymph flow and eventually may lead to lymphedema in the legs, scrotal area (for W bancrofti only), and arms.
Three diagnostic tests: Circulating filarial antigen assay; Blood smears (10pm-4am); PCR; Serology; Ultrasound and lymphoscintigraphic techniques
Organism for cellulitis: Streptococcus pyogenes. Dx: Acute Dermato-Lymphangio-Adenitis (ADLA). Attacks of ADLA are characterised by localized pain and tenderness, lymphadenitis and/or lymphangitis and/or cellulitis and local warmth, with (mostly 97% cases) or without systemic manifestations of fever, nausea and vomiting. Secondary infections due to bacteria like Group A streptococcus are responsible.
Three ways to prevent cellulitis: Control of edema/promotion of lymph flow; Rigorous hygiene/foot care; Good glycaemic control if diabetic; Long term antibiotics ("In patients with advanced stages of lymphedema, proper local care of the limb is not always possible due to deep skin folds or warty projections. If such patients have recurrent (=>2 episodes) ADLA attacks, long-term antibiotic therapy using oral penicillin or long acting benzathine penicillin 1.2 MU, deep IM every 3 weeks is indicated")

questions.model_answer:
a) Strongyloidiasis (Strongyloides stercoralis), with risk of hyperinfection given corticosteroid exposure. (The Loeffler-like pulmonary picture with eosinophilia in a patient on steroids is classic.)
b) (1) Stool - microscopy/agar plate culture for larvae (multiple samples). (2) Serum - Strongyloides serology (ELISA). (3) Sputum (or BAL) - examination for filariform larvae, especially in hyperinfection.

d) (1) Ivermectin 200 mcg/kg/day (extended/repeated in hyperinfection) - drug of choice. (2) Discontinue/minimize corticosteroids and immunosuppression; treat before starting steroids and screen at-risk patients.

parts.text: What is the risk of ivermectin?
Give two ways to manage a person from a Strongyloides-endemic region who is about to start immunosuppression.

parts_raw.text: A) What is the risk of ivermectin?
B) 2 ways to handle those from an endemic region for strongyloides going to start immunosuppression?

questions.model_answer:
a) In a patient co-infected with Loa loa who has high-level microfilaremia, ivermectin can precipitate a severe, potentially fatal encephalopathy; therefore screen for Loa loa before giving ivermectin in Loa-endemic areas and use albendazole as an alternative if heavy loiasis is confirmed.
b) (1) Screen ("test") – serology for Strongyloides (and stool studies) and treat those who are positive with ivermectin before starting immunosuppression. (2) Empiric ("presumptive") treatment – give ivermectin to at-risk patients before, or without waiting for, test results, given the high mortality of steroid-induced hyperinfection.
questions.beyond_mandell: The ivermectin–Loa loa encephalopathy risk is from filariasis/loiasis literature (Mandell filariasis chapter, WHO), not this intestinal-nematode chapter, which only establishes that steroids/immunosuppression precipitate Strongyloides hyperinfection. The screen-and-treat vs empiric-treat strategies are standard pre-immunosuppression Strongyloides practice.

cohort_answer.text: A) Administration of ivermectin to highly loa loa microfilaremic subjects can precipitate life-threatening encephalopathy. Relative contraindications: confirmed/suspected loa loa infection (albendazole alternative), previous hypersensitivity, weight<15kg or age<1 year, pregnant women (category C). B) 'Test and treat' approach; empiric administration of ivermectin to at-risk patients before immunosuppression before results are back.

(2) Lymphatic filariasis / occult filarial infection (Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia spp.) given endemic India origin. (3) Schistosomiasis (chronic tissue helminth causing persistent eosinophilia). b) (1) Strongyloides serology (IgG ELISA) - more sensitive than stool. (2) Filarial studies: nocturnal (10pm-2am) blood smear for microfilariae plus filarial serology (antifilarial IgG4) or circulating antigen. (3) Schistosoma serology, and HIV serology as a contributor/coinfection to screen.

cohort_answer.text: A) Strongyloides stercoralis; Schistosomiasis; HIV; Helminths (filariasis). B) HIV serology; Strongyloides serology; Schistosoma serology; Stool ova + parasite; Filarial serology.

questions.model_answer: a) Wuchereria bancrofti (the predominant cause of lymphatic filariasis in India; Brugia malayi is an alternative). b) Adult worms reside in the lymphatics of the spermatic cord/lower limb; worm death and chronic inflammation cause lymphatic dilatation, obstruction, and impaired drainage, leading to hydrocele/scrotal lymphedema. c) (1) Nocturnal (10pm-2am) thick blood smear for microfilariae. (2) Filarial antigen test (circulating W. bancrofti antigen) or antifilarial IgG4 serology. (3) Scrotal/lymphatic ultrasound showing the "filarial dance sign" of motile adult worms. d) Acute bacterial cellulitis / acute dermatolymphangioadenitis of the lymphedematous limb. e) Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes); Staphylococcus aureus is also possible. f) (1) Meticulous skin/foot hygiene and treatment of entry lesions including interdigital tinea. (2) Limb care: compression/elevation, exercise, and lymphedema management. (3) Prophylactic penicillin for recurrent episodes.
questions.beyond_mandell: WHO lymphatic filariasis morbidity-management guidance for limb care and penicillin prophylaxis.

cohort_answer.text: A) Wuchereria bancrofti; Brugia malayi; Brugia timori. B) Adult worms live in afferent lymphatics of lower extremities and male genitalia causing inflammation and obstruction to lymphatic flow. C) Filarial serology for IgG1 and IgG4; nocturnal blood smear (10pm-2am); scrotal US for filarial dance sign (Lombarda sign). D) Leg cellulitis. E) Group A Strep or S. aureus. F) Wound care; compression stockings; treat tinea; penicillin ppx if recurrent; for lymphedema - physio, postural drainage, compression.

questions.question: For each of the following, indicate whether you would use steroids as adjunctive therapy (yes or no): tuberculous meningitis; neurocysticercosis with a viable intraparenchymal cyst; cerebral malaria; acute schistosomiasis; a large echinococcal cyst at risk of rupture during PAIR.
questions.question_raw: For each of the following, list if you would use steroids as adjunctive therapy (yes or no): TB meningitis; Neurocysticercosis with viable intraparenchymal cyst; Cerebral malaria; Acute schistosomiasis; Large echinococcal cyst with risk of rupture during PAIR.

parts.text: Indicate yes/no for steroid use in each scenario with rationale.

parts_raw.text: Indicate yes/no for steroid use in each scenario and rationale

questions.model_answer: (1) TB meningitis: YES - adjunctive dexamethasone reduces mortality in confirmed TBM (not HIV+, where evidence is weaker). Note: steroids are NOT routine during purely empirical/diagnostic therapy as they blunt the clinical and CSF response and can worsen an undiagnosed fungal infection. (2) Neurocysticercosis with viable intraparenchymal cyst: YES - corticosteroids control the peri-lesional inflammation/edema provoked by antiparasitic (albendazole) therapy; not indicated for calcified cysts with isolated edema. (3) Cerebral malaria: NO - randomized data show steroids are harmful (prolonged coma, more complications). (4) Acute schistosomiasis (Katayama / acute neuroschistosomiasis): YES - corticosteroids given with praziquantel to suppress the hypersensitivity reaction. (5) Large echinococcal cyst at risk of rupture during PAIR: NO - no role for adjunctive steroids; risk is anaphylaxis, managed with antihistamines/epinephrine and peri-procedural albendazole, not steroids.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the TB-meningitis point is touched in this chapter (p. 1225, advising against routine steroids during empirical therapy). Steroid use in confirmed TBM, neurocysticercosis, cerebral malaria, schistosomiasis, and echinococcosis/PAIR rests on IDSA/WHO guidance and the respective Mandell disease chapters, not the chronic meningitis chapter.

cohort_answer.text: Katayama fever (acute schisto) - yes (5 days pred 40mg followed by praziquantel per Mandell's). Neurocysticercosis intraventricular lesions not calcified and no hydrocephalus - yes (dexamethasone 6-8mg/day divided TID for 28 days, then slow taper over 2-8 weeks; not indicated in calcified cysts with isolated perilesional edema; steroids lower praziquantel levels and increase albendazole levels, partial reason for albendazole use in limited CNS disease). TB meningitis - yes (non-HIV TB pericarditis can also use steroids, not for pleural; if HIV+ insufficient evidence). Ruptured echinococcus - no (not addressed in guidelines or UpToDate). Cerebral malaria - no

questions.model_answer: a) Wuchereria bancrofti (accounts for ~90% of cases). b) Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia. c) Elevated antifilarial antibody (antifilarial IgG/IgG4) - the confirmatory serologic test; peripheral eosinophilia is markedly high while microfilariae are typically absent from blood. d) (1) Lymphedema/elephantiasis. (2) Hydrocele (chyluria is a further complication).

cohort_answer.text: Most common cause: Wuchereria bancrofti (90% of cases). Clinical syndrome: Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia. Confirmatory test: Blood smear evening for microfilariae; Serology (DEC is treatment x1 dose). Chronic complications: Lymphedema; Hydrocele; Chyluria

questions.model_answer: Onchocerca volvulus (river blindness), a tissue nematode transmitted by the Simulium (black fly) near fast-flowing rivers; microfilariae migrating to the cornea cause sclerosing keratitis and blindness. Treatment is ivermectin, which is contraindicated/used with caution in Loa loa coinfection given the risk of fatal encephalopathy.

cohort_answer.text: Onchocerca volvulus. Tissue nematode. Typically found in Central Africa, also Western/Eastern Africa, near rivers where Simulium Black Fly is present (bites typically during the day). Can progress from subcutaneous tissue to lymph nodes and cornea, causing keratitis and blindness. Treatment: Ivermectin (contraindicated in Loa loa co-infection as can cause fatal encephalitis; if so, use Doxycycline + Albendazole then possibly DEC).
